unit.reading: As I am about to demonstrate a most philosophical proposition—whether devout reason is absolute master over the passions—I would rightly advise you to pay earnest attention to philosophy.
For the discourse is both necessary to knowledge for everyone and, moreover, it contains the praise of the greatest virtue, namely, prudence.
If, then, reason appears to master the passions that hinder self-control, namely gluttony and lust,
it also evidently exercises mastery over the passions that obstruct justice, such as malice, and over those that obstruct courage, namely anger, fear, and pain.
How is it then, some might perhaps ask, if reason rules the passions, that it does not master forgetfulness and ignorance? They attempt a ridiculous argument.
For reason does not rule over its own passions, but over those that oppose justice, courage, and self-control; and over these not so as to destroy them, but so as not to yield to them.
From many other sources, therefore, I could demonstrate to you that reason is sovereign over the passions,
but I could prove this far more clearly from the noble courage of those who died for virtue—Eleazar, the seven brothers, and their mother.
For all of these, despising pains unto death, demonstrated that reason has full mastery over the passions.
It is fitting for me to praise for their virtues the men who died with their mother at that time for the sake of noble goodness, and for their honors I would pronounce them blessed.

For having been admired not only by all people for their courage and endurance, but even by their torturers, they became the cause of the downfall of the tyranny against the nation, having conquered the tyrant by their endurance so that their homeland was purified through them.

Now it will be possible to speak immediately about these things after beginning with the proposition, as is my custom, and in this manner I will turn to the narrative concerning them, giving glory to the all-wise God.
We inquire, then, whether reason is sovereign over the passions.
Let us define what reason is and what passion is, how many kinds of passions there are, and whether reason masters all of them.
Reason, then, is the mind accompanied by right judgment, preferring the life of wisdom.
Wisdom, therefore, is the knowledge of divine and human matters and of their causes.
This, in turn, is the education of the Law, through which we learn divine matters reverently and human matters beneficially.
The forms of wisdom are prudence, justice, courage, and self-control.
Most authoritative of all is prudence, by means of which reason masters the passions.
The two most comprehensive natures of the passions are pleasure and pain; and each of these pertains naturally both to the body and to the soul.
Many attendant passions are associated with both pleasure and pain.
Prior to pleasure there is desire, and after pleasure there is joy.
Prior to pain there is fear, and after pain there is grief.
Anger is a passion common to both pleasure and pain, if one considers how it befalls someone.
Within pleasure there is also the malicious disposition, which is the most manifold of all passions:
pertaining to the soul are arrogance, love of money, love of glory, contentious rivalry, and envy;
and pertaining to the body are indiscriminate eating, gluttony, and solitary eating.
Just as pleasure and pain are two plants of the body and soul, there are many offshoots of these plants,
each of which the master-gardener reason, by pruning, trimming, binding up, irrigating, and redirecting in every way, tames the thickets of character and passions.
For reason is the guide of the virtues and the sovereign over the passions. Observe, therefore, first through the actions that hinder self-control that reason is absolute master over the passions.
Self-control, then, is mastery over the desires;
and of the desires, some are of the soul, others of the body, and reason appears to master both of these.
For otherwise, when moved toward forbidden foods, how do we turn away from the pleasures derived from them? Is it not because reason is able to master the appetites? I certainly think so.
Therefore, when we desire water creatures, birds, four-footed animals, and all kinds of foods that are forbidden to us according to the Law, we abstain through the mastery of reason.
For the passions of the appetites are restrained, being checked by the temperate mind, and all the impulses of the body are muzzled by reason.
And what wonder is it if the soul's desires for participation in beauty are nullified?
At any rate, the temperate Joseph is praised for this reason, that by his understanding he mastered pleasure.
For being young and in the prime of youth for sexual union, he nullified the spur of the passions by reason.
And reason appears to master not only the frenzied urge of pleasure, but every desire as well.
For the law says, "You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor anything that belongs to your neighbor."
And yet, when the law tells us not to covet, I could persuade you all the more that reason is able to master desires, just as it can master the passions that hinder justice.
For in what way is a person who is by disposition a solitary eater, a glutton, or even a drunkard reformed, unless it is evident that reason is master of the passions?

Accordingly, one who lives according to the law, even if he is a lover of money, immediately does violence to his own disposition by lending to the needy without interest and canceling the debt when the sabbatical year arrives.

And even if someone is stingy, he is restrained by the law through reason, neither gleaning the harvest crops nor stripping the remaining grapes from the vineyards. And in other matters as well, one can recognize this, that reason is master of the passions.
For the law also masters affection toward parents, not betraying virtue on their account;
and it prevails over love for a wife, reproving her when she breaks the law;
and it rules over affection for children, punishing them for wickedness;
and it dominates intimacy with friends, rebuking them for evil.

And do not consider it strange if reason is able to master even enmity on account of the law, neither cutting down the cultivated trees of enemies, but preserving the lost property of enemies for those who lost it and helping to raise up what has fallen.
Reason is also shown to rule over the more violent passions: love of power, vainglory, boastfulness, arrogance, and envy.
For the temperate mind repels all these malevolent passions, just as it also does anger; for indeed it masters it.
At least, when Moses was angry with Dathan and Abiram, he did nothing against them in anger, but governed his anger by reason.
For the temperate mind is able, as I said, to triumph over the passions, altering some and nullifying others.
Otherwise, why did our all-wise father Jacob blame Simeon and Levi and their companions for slaughtering the Shechemites as a whole nation without reason, saying, "Cursed be their anger"?
For if reason were not able to master anger, he would not have spoken thus.
For when God fashioned man, he implanted his passions and inclinations;
and at that time, over all things, he enthroned the sacred guiding mind through the sense organs,
and to this he gave a law, by living according to which it will rule over a kingdom that is temperate, just, good, and courageous.
How then, someone might say, if reason is master of the passions, does it not control forgetfulness and ignorance?
Now this argument is entirely ridiculous; for reason does not appear to master its own passions, but those of the body.
For instance, no one can eradicate desire from us, but reason can ensure that we are not enslaved to desire.
No one can eradicate anger from the soul, but it is possible for reason to come to the aid of anger.
No one can eradicate malice from us, but reason can serve as an ally so that we are not bent by malice.
For reason is not the uprooter of the passions, but their adversary.
This can be considered more clearly through the thirst of King David.
For when David, having attacked the foreigners for a whole day, had killed many of them along with the soldiers of the nation,
then, when evening came, sweating and exceedingly exhausted, he came to the royal tent, around which the entire army of our ancestors was encamped.
Now all the others were at dinner,
but the king, being intensely thirsty, although he had springs in abundance, was not able to satisfy his thirst with them;
rather, a certain irrational desire for the water with the enemy, growing intense, parched him and, consuming him, burned him up.

Wherefore, while the bodyguards were complaining about the king’s desire, two robust young soldiers, respecting the king’s desire, put on full armor, took a pitcher, and crossed over the enemy’s ramparts.
And slipping past the sentries at the gates, they went searching throughout the whole camp of the enemy.
And having found the spring, they boldly brought the drink from it to the king.
He, however, though burning with thirst, reasoned that a drink considered equivalent to blood was a terrible danger to his soul.
Therefore, setting reason against desire, he poured out the drink as a libation to God.
For the temperate mind is capable of conquering the compulsions of the passions and extinguishing the flames of frenzied urges,
and of wrestling down bodily pains even when extreme, and by the moral excellence of reason of spitting upon all the dominations of the passions.
And now the moment calls us to the demonstration of the story of temperate reason.

For when our ancestors enjoyed profound peace because of their observance of the law and were faring well, so that even Seleucus Nicanor, the king of Asia, both set aside funds for them for the sacrificial service and approved their way of government,
then certain individuals, rebelling against the common harmony, brought about manifold disasters.

For a certain Simon, who was a political opponent of Onias—who then held the high priesthood for life, a noble and good man—since he was unable to harm him by slandering him in every way concerning the nation, went into exile in order to betray his homeland.
Coming therefore to Apollonius, the governor of Syria, Phoenicia, and Cilicia, he said:

"Being loyal to the king’s interests, I have come to disclose that many tens of thousands of private funds are stored in the treasuries of Jerusalem, not shared with the sacred accounts, and that these belong to King Seleucus."
When Apollonius learned each of these things, he praised Simon for his devotion to the king, and going up to Seleucus, he disclosed the hoard of money.
And having received authority over these matters, he quickly came to our homeland with the accursed Simon and a very heavy army;
and approaching, he said that he had come by the king’s commands in order to take the private money from the treasury.

And when the nation protested and objected to his statement, considering it an outrage if those who had entrusted their deposits to the sacred treasury should be deprived of them, they hindered him as best they could.
But with threats Apollonius proceeded to the temple.
And while the priests, together with women and children, supplicated God in the temple to defend the holy place that was being treated with contempt,
and as Apollonius was going up with his armed force to plunder the money, angels on horseback appeared from heaven, flashing with their weapons and striking great fear and trembling into them.

Apollonius at any rate fell down half-dead in the temple enclosure that was open to all nations, stretched out his hands to heaven, and with tears pleaded with the Hebrews to pray for him and propitiate the heavenly host.
For he said that he had sinned so as to deserve even death, and that if saved, he would sing the praise of the blessedness of the holy place to all humanity.
Moved by these words, Onias the high priest, though otherwise cautious lest King Seleucus should think Apollonius had been destroyed by human intrigue and not by divine justice, prayed for him.
And he, having been miraculously preserved, departed to report to the king what had happened to him.
When King Seleucus died, his son Antiochus Epiphanes succeeded to the throne, an arrogant and terrible man,
who deposed Onias from the high priesthood and appointed his brother Jason as high priest,
who had agreed to pay three thousand six hundred and sixty talents annually if he would confer the office upon him.
And he permitted him both to serve as high priest and to govern the nation.
And he corrupted the nation's way of living and transformed their constitution toward every form of lawlessness,
so that he not only constructed a gymnasium on the very citadel of our homeland, but also abolished the guardianship of the temple.
Indignant at these things, divine justice incited Antiochus himself to wage war against them.
For while he was waging war in Egypt against Ptolemy, and heard that when a rumor had spread of his death the people of Jerusalem rejoiced exceedingly, he quickly marched against them;
and having plundered them, he issued a decree that if any of them should be seen living according to the ancestral law, they should die.
And when he was in no way able through his decrees to destroy the nation’s observance of the law, but saw all his own threats and punishments nullified,
so that even women were hurled down from cliffs along with their infants because they had circumcised their children, though they knew beforehand that they would suffer this—
Since, therefore, his decrees were despised by the people, he personally compelled each member of the nation through tortures to taste defiled food and renounce Judaism.
The tyrant Antiochus, having seated himself with his counselors upon a high place, with his armed forces standing around him in a circle,
ordered the spearmen to drag forward each and every Hebrew and compel them to taste swine's flesh and food sacrificed to idols;
and if any were unwilling to eat the defiled food, to break them on the wheel and put them to death.

When many had been seized, one first from the herd named Eleazar, a priest by lineage, a lawyer by training, advanced in years, and known to many of those around the tyrant because of his age, was brought near him.
And seeing him, Antiochus said,
"Before I begin the tortures against you, old man, I would advise you to taste the pork and save your life;
for I respect your age and your gray hair, which you have possessed for so long a time, though you do not seem to me to be a philosopher while practicing the religion of the Jews.
For why do you abhor eating the flesh of this animal, when nature has graciously bestowed it as the most excellent?
For it is senseless not to enjoy pleasant things that bring no reproach, and unjust to turn away from the gifts of nature.
But it seems to me you will act even more senselessly if, holding vain notions about truth, you go on to despise me also, to your own punishment.
Will you not wake up from your nonsensical philosophy, scatter the rubbish of your reasonings, adopt a mindset worthy of your age, and philosophize according to the truth of what is expedient,
and, paying homage to my humane counsel, have pity on your own old age?
For consider that even if there is some watchful power over this religion of yours, it would pardon you for any transgression committed through compulsion."
While the tyrant was urging him in this manner to the unlawful eating of flesh, Eleazar asked leave to speak,
and having received permission to speak, he began to address him thus:
"We, Antiochus, who are convinced that we live under a divine law, consider no compulsion to be more forcible than our obedience to the law;
therefore we deem it right under no circumstances to transgress it.
And yet, even if our law were not truly divine, as you suppose, but we had otherwise believed it to be divine, not even so would it be permissible for us to nullify our reputation for piety.
Do not think, therefore, that this would be a small sin if we were to eat defiled food;
for transgressing in small things and in great things has equal force,
for in both cases alike the law is despised.
You mock our philosophy as if we were not living by sound reason under it;
yet it thoroughly teaches us self-control, so that we master all pleasures and desires, and trains us in courage, so that we willingly endure every pain,
and it instructs us in justice, so that through all our conduct we maintain equality, and it teaches piety, so that we revere the only existing God magnificently.
Therefore we do not eat defiled food; for believing that the law is established by God, we know that the Creator of the world has compassion for our nature in giving us the law;
he has permitted us to eat things that are suitable to our souls, but has forbidden us to eat meat that would be harmful.
It is tyrannical not only to compel us to transgress, but also to eat, so that you may mock us for this most hateful eating of defiled food.
But you will not laugh this laugh at me,
nor will I disregard the sacred oaths of our ancestors concerning the keeping of the law,
not even if you gouge out my eyes and burn out my entrails.
I am not so old and unmanly that my reason does not remain youthful for the sake of piety.
Therefore prepare the wheels and blow the fire more violently!
I do not pity my own old age so much that I would through my own action break the ancestral law.
I will not prove false to you, Law our instructor, nor will I renounce you, beloved self-control!"
Nor will I disgrace you, philosophical reason, nor will I disown you, honorable priesthood and knowledge of the Law.
Neither shall you defile the revered mouth of my old age, nor the full age of a life lived according to the Law.
My ancestors will receive me pure, not having feared your compulsions even unto death.
For you may tyrannize over the ungodly, but over my reasonings in defense of godliness you will be master neither by words nor by deeds.
When he had answered the tyrant's persuasions in this manner, the guards standing by dragged Eleazar bitterly to the instruments of torture.
And first they stripped the old man, who was adorned with the dignity of godliness;
then, binding his arms behind him on both sides, they scourged him with whips,
while a herald on the other side called out, "Obey the commands of the king!"
But the truly magnanimous and noble Eleazar, as though being tortured in a dream, was in no way turned aside;
instead, lifting his eyes high toward heaven, the old man had his flesh shredded by the whips, drenched with blood, while his ribs were laid open with wounds.
And falling to the ground because his body could not bear the agonies, he still kept his reasoning upright and unswerving.
Indeed, one of the cruel guards leaped upon him and kicked him in the flanks to make him rise up as he fell.
Yet he endured the pains, held the compulsion in contempt, and persevered through the torments;
and like a noble athlete being beaten, the old man conquered his torturers.
With his face running with sweat and panting heavily, he was admired even by his torturers for his courage.
Wherefore, partly in pity for his old age,
partly out of the sympathy of long acquaintance, and partly in admiration of his endurance, some of the king's attendants approached him and said,
"Why, Eleazar, do you senselessly destroy yourself with these evils?
We will set before you some of the cooked meats; you just pretend to taste the swine's flesh, and be saved!"
And Eleazar, as if tortured more bitterly by this advice, cried out:
"May we, the children of Abraham, never think so wickedly as to turn cowardly and act out a role unbecoming to us!
For it would be irrational if we, having lived a life of truth until old age and having lawfully preserved its reputation, should now change our course,
and we ourselves should become a pattern of impiety to the young, setting an example of eating defiled food.
And it is disgraceful if we should survive for a short time, and that while being derided by all for cowardice,
and despised by the tyrant as unmanly, failing to defend our divine Law even unto death.
Therefore, O children of Abraham, die nobly for godliness!
And you, guards of the tyrant, why do you delay?"
Seeing him so high-minded against tortures and not even changing in response to their pity, they led him to the fire.
There, burning him with malicious instruments, they threw him down upon it and poured foul-smelling liquids into his nostrils.
And when he was already burned to the bones and about to expire, he lifted his eyes to God and said,
"You know, O God, that though I could save myself, I am dying in burning torments for the sake of the Law.
Be merciful to your nation, being satisfied with our punishment on their behalf.
Make my blood their purification, and take my life as a ransom for theirs."
And having said this, the holy man died nobly in the midst of the tortures, and even to the agonies of death resisted through reasoning for the sake of the Law.
Admittedly, therefore, devout reason is master over the passions.
For if the passions had mastered reason, we would have attributed to them the testimony of mastery;
but now, since reason has conquered the passions, we properly ascribe to it the authority of preeminence.
And it is right for us to confess that the mastery belongs to reason, since it prevails even over external pains—for to deny it would indeed be ridiculous.
And I demonstrate not only that reason has mastered pains, but also that it masters pleasures and yields to them in nothing.
For just like an excellent pilot, the reason of our father Eleazar, steering the ship of piety on the sea of passions
and though buffeted by the threats of the tyrant and inundated by the raging waves of tortures,
in no way turned the rudders of piety until he sailed into the harbor of immortal victory.

No besieged city ever held out against so many and varied war engines as did that all-holy man. Having his sacred soul consumed by tortures and racks, he conquered the besiegers through the reason that shielded his piety.
For father Eleazar, extending his mind like a projecting cliff, broke the raging surges of the passions.
O priest worthy of the priesthood, you did not defile your holy teeth, nor did you profane with defiling food the stomach that had made room for reverence toward God and purity.
O you who were in harmony with the Law and a philosopher of a divine life!
Such ought to be those who execute the Law, defending it with their own blood and noble sweat against sufferings unto death.

You, father, confirmed our good order of Law unto glory through your endurance, and by speaking with reverence of our sacred rites did not abolish them, and by your deeds authenticated the words of your divine philosophy,
O old man more powerful than tortures, elder more unyielding than fire, and great king over passions, Eleazar!
For just as father Aaron, armed with the censer, ran through the multitude of the people and overcame the fiery angel,
so Eleazar, the descendant of Aaron, while being consumed by the fire, did not change his reasoning.
And yet—most wonderful of all—though he was an old man, with the vigor of his body already dissolved, his flesh slackened, and his sinews worn out, he became young again
in spirit through reason, and by an Isaac-like reason nullified the many-headed rack.
O blessed old age, and venerable gray hair, and law-abiding life, which the faithful seal of death brought to perfection!
If, then, an old man despised tortures unto death for the sake of piety, devout reason is confessedly sovereign over the passions.
Perhaps some might say, "Not all master the passions, because not all possess prudent reason."
Yet as many as cultivate piety with all their heart, these alone are able to master the passions of the flesh,
believing that to God they do not die, just as neither did our patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, but they live to God.
Therefore, the fact that some appear to be mastered by passions on account of weak reason is no objection;
for who, philosophizing according to the complete standard of philosophy and having put trust in God,
and knowing that it is blessed to endure all toil for the sake of virtue, would not master the passions on account of reverence for God?
For only the wise and courageous person is master of the passions.
For this reason, even youths, philosophizing with the reason of piety, prevailed over more severe tortures.

For when the tyrant was conspicuously defeated in the first trial, being unable to compel an old man to eat defiling food, then indeed in great fury he ordered others from the Hebrew captives to be brought, and if they ate defiling food, to release them once they had eaten, but if they objected, to torture them more bitterly.
When the tyrant had given these orders, seven brothers were brought forward along with their aged mother, handsome, modest, noble, and charming in every way.
When the tyrant saw them surrounding their mother in their midst as if in a chorus, he was pleased with them; struck by their comeliness and nobility, he smiled at them and, calling them near, said:

"Young men, I admire each one of you with good will, and holding in high regard the beauty and number of so many brothers, I not only advise you not to display the same madness as the old man who was previously tortured, but I also urge you to yield to me and enjoy my friendship;
for just as I am able to punish those who disobey my commands, so also can I confer benefits upon those who obey me.
Trust me, then, and you shall receive positions of leadership over my affairs once you have renounced your ancestral ordinance of government;
and by adopting the Greek way of life and changing your manner of living, revel in your youth!"
For if you provoke me to anger by your disobedience, you will compel me to destroy each one of you with terrible punishments through torture.
Pity yourselves, therefore, since even I, your enemy, have compassion on your youth and your beauty.
Will you not consider this, that if you disobey nothing is in store for you except dying on the rack?
As he said this, he ordered the instruments of torture to be brought forward, so that fear might persuade them to eat defiled food.

When the guards had brought out wheels and joint-breakers, racks and pulleys, catapults and cauldrons, pans and finger-crushers, iron claws, wedges, and the braziers of fire, the tyrant continued and said:
“Be afraid, young men, and the Justice that you revere will be merciful to you if you transgress under compulsion.”

Although they heard these enticements and saw these dreadful things, they were not only not afraid, but they philosophized in opposition to the tyrant and by their sound reasoning destroyed his tyranny.
Yet let us consider: if any among them had been faint-hearted and unmanly, what kind of words would they have used? Would they not be these?
“O wretched and utterly foolish that we are! When the king calls us and appeals to us with beneficence if we obey him,
why do we cheer ourselves with vain intentions and dare a fatal disobedience?
Shall we not fear the instruments of torture, my brothers, and consider the threats of torments, and flee from this vainglory and destructive arrogance?
Let us take pity on our own youth and have compassion on our mother’s old age,
and let us bear in mind that if we disobey we shall die.
Even divine Justice will pardon us for fearing the king out of necessity.
Why do we banish ourselves from this most pleasant life and deprive ourselves of the sweet world?
Let us not resist necessity, nor vaingloriously seek our own racking.
Not even the Law itself voluntarily condemns us to death if we fear the instruments of torture.
Why has such contentiousness been instilled in us, and why does this fatal endurance please us, when it is possible to live untroubled if we obey the king?”
Yet the young men who were about to be tortured said none of these things, nor did they even contemplate them.
For they looked down on the passions and were masters over the pains,
so that as soon as the tyrant ceased advising them to eat defiled food, they all said together with one voice, as if from a single soul:
“Why do you delay, O tyrant? For we are ready to die rather than transgress our ancestral commandments.
For we would rightly be ashamed before our ancestors if we did not show obedience to the Law and follow Moses as our counselor.
Counselor of lawlessness, tyrant, do not pity us out of hatred for us more than we pity ourselves!
For we consider your pity, offered for our lawless survival, to be harder to bear than death itself.
You try to terrify us by threatening death through tortures, as if you had not learned just a short time ago from Eleazar.

If the old men of the Hebrews, enduring tortures for the sake of piety, maintained their godliness, all the more justly should we young men die, despising the tortures of your compulsions, which our elderly instructor has already conquered.
Test us then, tyrant! And if you put our lives to death on account of our piety, do not think that you harm us by torturing us.
For we, through this suffering and endurance, shall possess the prizes of virtue and shall be with God, for whose sake we also suffer;
but you, on account of your bloodthirsty murder of us, will endure eternal torment by fire at the hands of divine Justice.”
When they had said this, the tyrant was not only indignant as against the disobedient, but was also enraged as against ingrates.
Therefore, at his command, the guards brought forward the eldest of them; and having torn off his tunic, they bound his hands and arms on each side with thongs.
When they had grown weary of flogging him with whips without accomplishing anything, they hoisted him onto the wheel,
around which the noble young man was stretched until his limbs were dislocated.
And as he was broken in every limb, he denounced him, saying:
Most polluted tyrant, enemy of heavenly justice, and cruel-minded, you do not maltreat me in this manner because I am a murderer or ungodly, but because I am a defender of the divine law.
And when the guards said, “Agree to eat, so that you may be released from the tortures,”
he said, “Your wheel is not so powerful, you vile ministers, that it can choke my reason! Cut my limbs, burn my flesh, and twist my joints!
For through all these tortures I will convince you that the children of the Hebrews alone are invincible for the sake of virtue.”
As he was saying this, they spread fire beneath him and tightened the wheel still further.
And the wheel was smeared on all sides with blood, the heap of coals was extinguished by the dripping of bodily fluids, and his flesh was torn away around the axles of the machine.
Even though the framework of his bones was already broken around him, the noble-minded and Abrahamic youth did not groan;
but as if being transformed by fire into immortality, he nobly endured the racks,
saying, “Imitate me, brothers! Do not desert my contest, nor disown our brotherhood of courageous spirit!
Fight a sacred and noble warfare on behalf of godliness, through which our just and ancestral Providence, becoming merciful to the nation, may punish the accursed tyrant.”
And having said this, the holy youth breathed his last.

While everyone marveled at his steadfastness of soul, the guards brought forward the next in age after the first, and having fastened iron hands with sharp claws on him, they bound him to the engine and the catapult.
And when, asking if he was willing to eat before being tortured, they heard his noble resolve,
the leopard-like beasts tore off all the flesh with the iron hands, dragging it from the sinews up to the chin, as well as the skin of his head. But enduring this severe pain, he said:
“How sweet is every manner of death for the sake of our ancestral religion!” And he said to the tyrant,
“Do you not think, most cruel of all tyrants, that you are being tortured more than I, seeing the arrogant reasoning of your tyranny defeated by our endurance for the sake of godliness?
For I lighten the pain by the pleasures that come through virtue,
while you are tortured amid the threats of your impiety. You will not escape, most abominable tyrant, the penalties of divine wrath.”
And after this one had endured a renowned death, the third was brought forward, being earnestly urged by many to taste and be saved.
But he cried out and said, “Do you not know that the same father begot me as those who died, and the same mother gave birth to me, and I was brought up on the same teachings?
I will not renounce the noble kinship of our brotherhood.”
Resenting the man’s boldness, with joint-dislocating instruments they dislocated his hands and feet, and prying them out of their sockets, they pulled his limbs apart,
breaking his fingers, his arms, his legs, and his elbows.
And being unable in any way to break his spirit, they stripped off the instruments and scalped him, tearing off the skin even to the tips of his fingers.
And immediately they led him to the wheel, around which, his vertebrae being dislocated, he saw his own flesh torn into shreds and drops of blood flowing down from his entrails.
And when he was about to die, he said,
“We, O most abominable tyrant, suffer these things for the sake of divine discipline and virtue;
but you, on account of your impiety and bloodthirstiness, will endure unceasing torments.”
And after he died in a manner worthy of his brothers, they dragged up the fourth, saying,
“Do not rage with the same madness as your brothers, but obey the king and save yourself!”
But he said to them, “You do not have a fire hot enough against me to make me play the coward.
By the blessed death of my brothers, the eternal destruction of the tyrant, and the everlasting life of the godly, I will not renounce our noble brotherhood!
Devise tortures, tyrant, so that through them also you may learn that I am a brother of those who were tortured before!”
Hearing this, bloodthirsty, murderous, and utterly defiled Antiochus ordered his tongue to be cut out.
But he said, “Even if you remove the organ of speech, God hears even those who are silent.
Look, my tongue is put out; cut it off! For you will not thereby cut out our reason.
Gladly are we maimed in the limbs of our body for God's sake.
God will speedily pursue you, for you cut out the tongue that sings divine praises.
When this one also had died, terribly abused by the tortures, the fifth leaped forward, saying:
“I am not about to beg off, tyrant, from the torture for the sake of virtue;
rather, I have come forward of my own accord, so that by killing me also you may owe to heavenly justice vengeance for even more crimes.
O hater of virtue and hater of mankind, what have we done that you destroy us in this manner?
Is it because we revere the Creator of all things and live according to his virtuous law?
Yet these things are worthy of honors, not tortures!”
While he was saying such things, the guards bound him and dragged him to the catapult,

on which they bound him at the knees, fastening them with iron fetters, and they bent his loins around a wheel-shaped wedge, around which his whole body was dismembered, bent back in the manner of a scorpion around the wheel.
Being in this manner constricted in breath and strangled in body,
he said, “Unwillingly, O tyrant, you bestow noble favors upon us, giving us the opportunity to demonstrate through nobler sufferings our endurance for the law.”
When he too had died, the sixth, a youth, was brought forward; and when the tyrant asked him whether he wished to eat and be released, he said:
“I am younger in age than my brothers, but of the same age in mind.
For having been born and raised for the same things, we ought also to die alike for the same things.
So if you are resolved to torture one who will not eat defiled food, torture!”
When he had said this, they led him to the wheel,
upon which, being thoroughly stretched and having his vertebrae dislocated, he was scorched with fire from below.
And heating sharp spits, they applied them to his back, and piercing his sides, they burned his entrails.
While being tortured he said, “O contest worthy of sacred honors, to which so many of us brothers have been summoned for a training in pain on behalf of godliness, and we have not been conquered!
For pious knowledge is invincible, O tyrant.
Armed with nobility, I too will die with my brothers,
I myself also bringing a great avenger upon you, O inventor of new tortures and enemy of those who are truly pious.
Six youths, we have overthrown your tyranny!
For your inability to alter our reason or to compel us to eat defiling food—is this not your overthrow?
Your fire is cold to us, your catapults cause no pain, and your violence is powerless.
For the guards who stand over us are not a tyrant's, but the divine law's; because of this, our reason is unconquerable.”
When he too had died blessedly, having been cast into a cauldron, the seventh came forward, the youngest of all.
The tyrant, taking pity on him, although he had been severely reviled by his brothers, and seeing him already wearing bonds, summoned him closer and tried to comfort him, saying:
“You see the end of your brothers' madness; for because of their disobedience they have been racked and died.
And you, if you do not comply, will be tortured, wretched boy, and will die before your time;
but if you comply, you will be a friend and will oversee the affairs of the kingdom.”

While urging these things, he sent for the boy's mother, so that, having pity on her who had been bereaved of so many sons, she might persuade the remaining one to the obedience that brings salvation.
And when his mother exhorted him in the Hebrew language, as we shall relate a little later,
"Release me," he said, "so that I may speak to the king and to all the Friends with him."
And rejoicing greatly at the boy's promise, they quickly untied him.
And running close to the pans,
he said, "Impious tyrant and most ungodly of all the wicked, were you not ashamed, having received your good things and the kingdom from God, to kill his servants and torture the champions of piety?
For this reason, Justice will reserve you for a denser and eternal fire and for torments that will never let you go for all eternity.

Were you not ashamed, though a human being yourself, you most beastly creature, to cut out the tongues of those of like nature who were made of the same elements, and to torture them having abused them in this way?
Indeed, though dying nobly, they fulfilled their piety toward God, but you will wail miserably for having unjustly killed the contenders for virtue."
And therefore, when about to die, he himself said:
"I will not desert the noble valor of my brothers,
and I call upon the God of our ancestors to be merciful to our nation.
But you he will punish both in this present life and after you have died."
And having prayed these words, he hurled himself into the pans, and so expired.
If, then, the seven brothers despised sufferings even unto death, it is universally agreed that devout reason is sovereign master over the passions.
For if they had been enslaved to the passions and eaten defiling food, we would say that they had been conquered by them.
Now, however, it is not so; but by the reason that is praised before God, they prevailed over the passions,
whose mastery of the mind cannot be overlooked, for they triumphed over both passion and pain.
How, then, is it not possible to acknowledge the power of reason over the passions among these men, who paid no heed to the agonies caused by fire?
For just as projecting towers of harbors, breaking the threats of the waves, provide a calm haven for those sailing in,
so the seven-towered right reason of the youths, having fortified the harbor of piety, conquered the tempestuous license of the passions.
For having formed a sacred chorus of piety, they encouraged one another, saying:
"Let us die like brothers, brothers, for the Law; let us imitate the three youths in Assyria who despised the furnace of equal affliction.
Let us not play the coward before the demonstration of piety."
And one said, "Courage, brother!" and another, "Endure nobly!"
And another, bringing it to remembrance, said, "Remember whence you came, and by the hand of what father Isaac endured being sacrificed for the sake of piety."

And each looking upon one another, all together cheerful and very courageous, said, "Let us consecrate ourselves with all our heart to God who gave us our lives, and let us surrender our bodies for the preservation of the Law.
Let us not fear him who thinks he is killing us,
for great is the soul's contest and the danger lying in eternal torment for those who transgress the commandment of God.
Therefore, let us arm ourselves with divine reason's mastery over the passions.
For if we die in this manner, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob will receive us, and all the patriarchs will praise us."
And to each one of their brothers as he was dragged away, the remaining ones would say, "Do not bring shame on us, brother, nor prove false to our brothers who have died before us!"
Now you are not ignorant of the charms of brotherhood, which divine and all-wise Providence has apportioned through fathers to those who are born, planting them through the maternal womb,
in which brothers reside for an equal length of time, being formed at the same time, nourished from the same blood, and brought to maturity through the same life-force,
and brought forth after equal periods, drinking milk from the same springs, from which embrace affectionate souls are nurtured together;
and they grow all the stronger through common rearing, daily association, other education, and our training in the law of God.
Since brotherly love was thus so deeply sympathetic, the seven brothers held an even deeper sympathy for one another.
For having been educated in the same Law, having practiced the same virtues, and having been reared together in a righteous life, they loved one another all the more.
For their common zeal for moral excellence intensified their goodwill and harmony toward one another;
for together with their piety, they made their brotherly affection more endearing to themselves.

Yet nevertheless, although nature, companionship, and the habits of virtue jointly increased the bonds of brotherhood among them, for the sake of piety the survivors endured seeing their brothers mistreated and tortured even to death,
even encouraging them toward the torture, so that they not only despised the pains, but also mastered the emotions of brotherly love.
O reasonings more royal than kings, and freer than the free!
O sacred and harmonious accord of the seven brothers concerning piety!
None of the seven youths showed cowardice or shrank from death,
but all, as though running on the path of immortality, hastened to death by tortures.
Just as the hands and feet move in harmony with the directions of the soul, so those holy youths, as if guided by the immortal soul of piety, agreed together to die on its behalf.
O all-holy group of seven harmonious brothers! For just as the seven days of the creation of the world circle about piety,
so the youths, dancing about the number seven, formed a circle and abolished the fear of tortures.

Even now we shudder when hearing of the affliction of those young men; but they, not only seeing, nor merely hearing the immediate words of threat, but even suffering, persevered—and that through the agonies of fire.
And what could be more painful than this? For the power of fire, being sharp and swift, quickly consumed their bodies.
And do not think it wondrous if reason prevailed over those men in the midst of tortures, when even a woman's mind despised still more diverse agonies;
for the mother of the seven youths endured the rackings inflicted on each one of her children.
Consider how manifold is the love of children, drawing everything toward heartfelt sympathy,
seeing that even irrational animals have a sympathy and affection for their offspring similar to that of human beings.
For among birds, the tame ones that frequent the roofs of houses shield their nestlings,
while those that build nests on mountain peaks and in the clefts of ravines and in the hollows and tops of trees hatch their young and ward off intruders;
and even if they cannot prevent them, flying around them in circles, grieving in their affection and calling out with their own voice, they help their young as best they can.
And why is it necessary to demonstrate through irrational animals their sympathy toward their young,
when even bees at the time of making wax defend themselves against intruders, and with their sting, as though with iron, strike those who approach their brood, warding them off even unto death?
Yet sympathy for her children did not sway the mother of the young men, who was of one mind with Abraham.
O reason, tyrant over the passions of children, and piety, more desirable to a mother than her children!
When two choices lay before her, piety and the temporary salvation of her seven sons according to the tyrant's promise,
she loved piety the more, which preserves unto eternal life according to God.

Oh, in what manner could I describe the parental passions of love for children? We impress a wondrous likeness of soul and form upon the tiny character of a child, especially because through feelings toward their offspring, mothers are more sympathetic than fathers.
For to the extent that mothers are more tender-hearted and prolific in bearing children, by so much the more do they love their children.
And of all mothers, the mother of the seven children was the most devoted to her children, having implanted affection for them through seven pregnancies,
and having been constrained to feel sympathy toward them through the many labor pains for each of them;
yet on account of the fear of God, she disregarded the temporary safety of her children.
Moreover, also because of the noble character of her sons and their obedience to the Law, she had a greater affection for them.

For they were righteous, self-controlled, courageous, magnanimous, loving toward their brothers, and devoted to their mother to such a degree that they obeyed her even unto death in observing the ordinances.

Yet nevertheless, although there were so many factors drawing the mother to sympathy through her love for her children, in the case of none of them were the all-diverse tortures able to turn her reason aside,
Instead, the mother exhorted each child individually and all of them together to death for the sake of piety.
O sacred nature, parental affection, love of offspring, nurture, and indomitable maternal passions!
Seeing each one racked and burned, the mother did not waver on account of piety.
She saw the flesh of her children melting in the fire, their fingers and toes writhing on the ground, and the skin of their heads down to their beards lying exposed like masks.
O mother, who experienced bitterer pangs now than the labor pains at their birth!
O woman, who alone brought forth whole and complete piety!
The firstborn breathing his last did not turn you aside, nor the second looking pitifully at you in his tortures, nor the third expiring,
nor did you weep when you beheld each one's eyes looking grimly under torture at the same torment and their nostrils signaling their approaching death.

When you saw child's flesh burned upon child's flesh, and severed hands upon hands, and severed heads upon heads, and corpse falling upon corpse, and saw the place made a common burial ground of your children through their tortures, you did not shed a tear.
Neither siren melodies nor swan songs draw listeners with delight as do the voices of children crying out to their mother amid tortures.
With what immense and numerous agonies was the mother then tortured as her sons were racked with wheels and cauteries!
Yet devout reason, having fortified her maternal feelings in the midst of these very sufferings, enabled her to disregard temporary parental love.
Although seeing the destruction of seven children and the intricate variety of the racks, the noble mother dissolved them all through faith in God.
For as in a council chamber within her own soul, seeing formidable counselors—nature, lineage, parental love, and the tortures of her children—
holding two ballots on behalf of her children, one bringing death and the other life,
the mother did not choose the deliverance that would save her seven sons for a short time,
but this daughter remembered the God-fearing endurance of Abraham.
O mother of the nation, vindicator of the law, defender of piety, and prize-winner in the contest fought through maternal love!
O you who were nobler than males in endurance, and more courageous than men in fortitude!
For just as the ark of Noah, carrying the world in the world-engulfing deluge, stoutly withstood the surging waves,
so you, guardian of the law, overwhelmed on every side in the flood of passions and battered by mighty winds—the tortures of your sons—nobly endured the storms for the sake of piety.
If, then, even a woman, advanced in years and the mother of seven children, endured watching the tortures of her offspring unto death, devout reason is confessedly sovereign over the passions.
I have demonstrated, then, that not only men have mastered the passions, but even a woman has despised the greatest tortures.

The lions around Daniel were not so fierce, nor was the furnace of Mishael ablaze with such ravenous fire, as burned the natural love for her children within her when she saw her seven sons tortured in such diverse ways.
Yet by the reason of piety the mother extinguished passions so great and so many.
Consider this as well: if the woman had been faint-hearted, being their mother, she would have lamented over them and perhaps spoken as follows:
“Ah, wretched me, and thrice-miserable many times over, who gave birth to seven sons and have become the mother of none!
O useless seven pregnancies, and profitless seven ten-month terms, and fruitless nursings, and wretched milk-feedings!
In vain, my children, have I endured many labor pains for you, and more arduous anxieties of rearing you!
Ah, some of my children unmarried, and those who married, to no purpose! I will not see your children, nor will I have the joy of being called grandmother.
O I, a woman once rich in children and blessed with noble sons, now a widow, alone and full of lamentation!
Nor if I die will I have any of my sons to bury me.”
Yet with no such dirge did the holy and God-fearing mother lament anyone, nor did she dissuade any of them lest they die, nor did she grieve as they were dying;
rather, having an adamantine mind and giving birth anew to her whole company of sons into immortality, she instead urged them on to death for the sake of piety, entreating them.
O mother, soldier of God for the sake of piety, elderly and a woman, through endurance you conquered even a tyrant, and you were found more powerful than a man in both deeds and words.
For indeed, when you were arrested with your children, you stood watching Eleazar being tortured and said to your children in the Hebrew language:
“O children, noble is the contest to which you have been called to bear witness for the nation; strive zealously for the ancestral Law!
For it would be disgraceful if this old man should endure the pains for the sake of piety, while you young men were terrified of the tortures.
Remember that because of God you received a share in the world and enjoyed life,
and for this reason you ought to endure every hardship for the sake of God,
for whose sake also our father Abraham hastened to sacrifice his son Isaac, the ancestor of our nation, and seeing his father's sword-bearing hand descending against him, Isaac did not cower.
And Daniel the righteous was thrown to the lions, and Ananias, Azarias, and Misael were hurled into the furnace of fire and endured for the sake of God.
Therefore, you too, having the same faith toward God, do not be distressed.
For it is unreasonable that those who know true piety should not resist the pains.”
By these words the mother of the seven, encouraging each one of her sons, persuaded them to die rather than transgress the commandment of God;
and even more, they knew this: that those who die for God live to God, just as Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the patriarchs.
Some of the bodyguards also said that when she was about to be seized to be put to death, in order that no one might touch her body, she threw herself into the pyre.
O mother, who with seven sons broke the tyrant’s violence, nullified his evil schemes, and demonstrated the nobility of faith!
For like a roof nobly supported upon the pillars of your children, you unswervingly endured the earthquake of the tortures.
Take courage, therefore, O holy-souled mother, holding firmly to the hope of endurance before God.
The moon is not as majestic in heaven with the stars as you have become honored before God, having guided your seven star-like sons toward piety, and you are established with them in heaven;
for your childbearing was from father Abraham.

If it were possible for us to paint, as on a tablet, the history of your piety, would not the onlookers shudder at the sight of a mother of seven children enduring various tortures even to death for the sake of piety?
For it would indeed be fitting to inscribe upon the tomb itself these words as a memorial for the members of our nation:
“Here an aged priest, an elderly woman, and seven sons are buried, having suffered through the violence of a tyrant who wished to destroy the way of life of the Hebrews;
they also vindicated their race, looking to God and enduring tortures even to death.”
For truly the contest fought by them was divine.
For at that time Virtue was the umpire, testing them through endurance; the prize of victory was incorruption in an everlasting life.
Eleazar competed first, the mother of the seven children entered the contest, and the brothers competed;
the tyrant was the antagonist, and the world and the human race were watching.
And piety conquered, crowning its own athletes.
Who did not marvel at the athletes of the divine legislation? Who was not astonished?
Indeed, the tyrant himself and his whole council marveled at their endurance,
because of which they now stand beside the divine throne and live the blessed eternity.
For Moses says, “And all the sanctified are under your hands.”
These, therefore, having been consecrated for God's sake, have been honored not only with this honor, but also in that because of them the enemy did not prevail over our nation,
and the tyrant was punished, and the homeland was purified, they having become, as it were, a ransom for the sin of the nation.
And through the blood of those devout people and the atoning sacrifice of their death, divine Providence preserved Israel, which had previously been afflicted.
For looking at the courage of their virtue and their endurance under tortures, the tyrant Antiochus proclaimed their endurance as an example to his soldiers,
and he found them noble and courageous for infantry battles and sieges, and by ravaging he conquered all his enemies.
O Israelite children, descendants of the seed of Abraham, obey this law and practice godliness in every way,
knowing that devout reason is master over the passions, not only over inward distresses, but also over outward pains.
For which reason, because they surrendered their bodies to sufferings for the sake of godliness, they were not only admired by men, but were also deemed worthy of a divine portion.
And because of them the nation enjoyed peace, and having revived the observance of the law in their homeland, they routed the enemy.

And the tyrant Antiochus was both punished on earth and is tormented after death; for when he was utterly unable to compel the people of Jerusalem to adopt foreign customs and depart from their ancestral practices, he then departed from Jerusalem and marched against the Persians.
The mother of the seven boys also spoke these righteous precepts to her children:
‘I was a pure virgin and did not leave my father's house, but guarded the rib that was built into woman.
No ravager of the wilderness ruined me, no seducer in the field, nor did the deceitful serpent defile the purity of my virginity.

I remained with my husband for the duration of my prime; and when these sons grew to maturity, their father died. Blessed indeed was he, for having lived out a life blessed with children, he was not grieved by a time of childlessness.
He used to teach you the Law and the Prophets while he was still with you.
He read to you of Abel, who was slain by Cain, and of Isaac, who was offered as a burnt offering, and of Joseph in prison.
He told you of the zealous Phinehas, and taught you about Ananias, Azarias, and Misael in the fire.
He glorified also Daniel in the lions' den, whom he pronounced blessed.
He also reminded you of the scripture of Isaiah, which says: “Even if you pass through fire, the flame shall not burn you.”
He sang to you the psalmist David, who says: “Many are the afflictions of the righteous.”
He quoted Solomon’s proverb to you, saying: “She is a tree of life to those who do his will.”
He confirmed Ezekiel, who says: “Shall these dry bones live?”
For he did not forget to teach the song that Moses taught, which says:
“I will kill and I will make alive; this is your life and the length of your days.”’

O bitter and yet not bitter was that day, when the bitter tyrant of the Greeks quenched fire with fire in his cruel caldrons, and with seething rage brought to the catapult and to his tortures the seven sons of the daughter of Abraham,
blinded the pupils of their eyes, cut out their tongues, and put them to death by various tortures.
For these crimes divine Justice pursued and will pursue that accursed tyrant.
But the children of Abraham, along with their triumphant mother, are gathered into the chorus of the ancestors, having received pure and immortal souls from God.
To whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
